result.Method of Attack: Spam packages published to inflate software developer contributions artificially via the Tea protocol; Use of gibberish/random package names, implausible dependencies, and transitive dependencies to game teaRank; Supply chain pollution by injecting spam packages as dependencies, including disguised dependencies (e.g., sournoise depending on spam package instead of axios); Artificial inflation of contribution metrics without redeeming quality; Potential to skew AI model training data with garbage packages
result.Impacted Systems: npm open-source ecosystem; Developers using npm packages; Open-source package registries (npm, Rubygems)
result.Attack Vector: Automated mass publication of spam packages exploiting Tea protocol incentives; Transitive dependencies pulling in spam packages without developer intent; Typosquatting and deceptive package naming to mimic legitimate packages
result.Indicators of Compromise: Presence of tea.yaml file identifying code owner; Gibberish or random word combination package names; Implausible dependency lists and high number of dependents; Packages like sournoise with misleading dependencies (e.g., axios dependency pointing to spam package URL https://registry.npmjs.org/@putrifransiska/kwonthol36/-/kwonthol36-1.1.4.tgz); High volume of new packages published daily (up to 48,000 on 8 April 2024); Packages named quasar-fig-0e1t, web3-cover, and others identified as spam
